AI workshop · Islands and Small States Institute

Working with Claude: a project folder, clear prompts and a website of your own

A practical morning for colleagues who are new to AI. Keep the Claude app open beside this presentation and work along with me.

Dr Roxane de WaeghMarie Skłodowska-Curie Postdoctoral FellowIslands and Small States InstituteUniversity of Malta

Before we start

Think of one task this week that took you longer than you expected. Write the task down.

An email you rewrote three times, the minutes of a meeting, a form for Finance, a reading you needed to summarise. You will use this task when we practise prompts.

What we build this morning

1Use Claude safely within the Pro plan
2Set up a project folder on your laptop
3Write two short instruction files
4Write a clear prompt for your own task
5Use Claude for procurement and travel forms
6Add a skill and publish a website, if time allows

How Claude works

Claude writes an answer one word at a time, choosing the word most likely to come next

Claude is writing
Illustration of the idea. The bars are not real figures.

Large language model

Trained on a very large amount of text

From that text Claude learned which words tend to follow which. Claude predicts the next word, adds the word to the answer and predicts again.

The risk

A fluent answer can still be wrong

When Claude does not know a reference, Claude can still write one that looks real but does not exist.

What to expect

Like NVivo, Claude makes the work faster. Neither tool can think for you.

What Claude does well

  • ✓Drafts emails, memos and minutes from your saved instructions
  • ✓Organises your folder and finds the right file
  • ✓Completes University forms from the templates you saved
  • ✓Reminds you of the small steps in a procedure
  • ✓Sets up scheduled reminders
  • ✓Checks your drafts against your own writing rules
  • ✓Builds presentations, charts and websites
  • ✓Writes code to clean data or count codes

What remains your work

  • ✕Judge which patterns in your data matter
  • ✕Build theory from patterns, through the interpretive reasoning that researchers use
  • ✕Judge whether a claim is true without your checking
  • ✕Know the unwritten rules of your field until you write the rules down
  • ✕Take responsibility for the work, which carries your name
Key tipNVivo sorts and counts your codes, but you decide what the themes are. Claude works the same way.

Using Claude safely

Check every fact, keep personal data out of Claude and declare how you used AI

Check

Open every reference yourself

  1. Copy the title of the reference Claude gave you.
  2. Paste the title into scholar.google.com.
  3. Check that the authors, year and journal match.
  4. Check every number against the original table.

Protect

Keep personal data out

Do not type or upload participant names, interview transcripts, student marks or health details, or anything your ethics approval covers. Anthropic’s servers process every file you share.

Declare

Say how you used AI

The University of Malta follows the European Research Area guidelines on the responsible use of generative AI in research. Journals and examiners may ask how you used AI, so keep a short note of what Claude did.

Key tipIf you cannot find a reference in Google Scholar, do not cite the reference.

The Pro plan

The Pro plan gives you an allowance every five hours and a larger allowance for the whole week

Current session0% used
Refills five hours after your first message
This week0% used
Refills once a week, on a fixed day

Both bars match the page under Settings > Usage. The amounts each task adds are an illustration, not Anthropic’s figures.

Press a task and watch the bars

Short questions use very little. Long chats, large files, web searches and building files use the most, because Claude reads and writes much more for each of those tasks.

Key tipStart a new chat for each new task. A long chat makes Claude reread everything above your message each time you write.

Project folders

A project folder gives Claude the same instructions at the start of every task

Without a project folder

Chat 1 · email

I am a researcher at ISSI. My project studies money sent home to small islands. Write formally, British spelling...

Now draft the email.

Chat 2 · minutes

I am a researcher at ISSI. My project studies money sent home to small islands. Write formally, British spelling...

Now write the minutes.

Chat 3 · report

I am a researcher at ISSI. My project studies money sent home to small islands. Write formally, British spelling...

Now draft the report.

The same paragraph typed again: 0 times

With a project folder

Chat 1 · email

Read from About my project.md

Draft the email.

Chat 2 · minutes

Read from About my project.md

Write the minutes.

Chat 3 · report

Read from About my project.md

Draft the report.

You write the paragraph once. Claude reads the file at the start of each task.

Anthropic. (2026b). Organize your tasks with projects in Claude Cowork. Claude Help Center. https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14116274-organize-your-tasks-with-projects-in-claude-cowork

Step one

Make one folder for your project on your laptop, with three folders inside

  1. Open Finder and click Documents in the left column.
  2. Click File in the top menu, then New Folder.
  3. Type My research project and press Return.
  4. Open the new folder with a double-click.
  5. Make three more folders inside: Instructions, Drafts and Finished.
  1. Open File Explorer and click Documents.
  2. Right-click an empty space and choose New, then Folder.
  3. Type My research project and press Enter.
  4. Open the new folder with a double-click.
  5. Make three more folders inside: Instructions, Drafts and Finished.

Step two

Connect the folder to Claude once, inside a project

In the Claude desktop app

  1. In the left panel, click Projects, then the + button.
  2. Choose Use an existing folder.
  3. Pick My research project in Documents.
  4. Give the project a name and write one sentence about what you are trying to achieve.
  5. Click Create.

The folder stays on your laptop. Claude can open only the folders you connect, and only while the desktop app is open.

Instruction files

An .md file is a plain text note that both you and Claude can read easily

What you type

What you and Claude see

#

A heading

One # makes a title. Two ## make a smaller heading.

- item

A list

A hyphen at the start of a line makes a bullet point.

.md

Markdown

The letters .md stand for Markdown. TextEdit or Notepad opens the file on any laptop.

Instruction file one

About my project.md tells Claude who you are before every task

# About my project
## Who I am
I am a researcher at the Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.Your role
## What my project is about
My project studies how families on small islands use money sent home by relatives abroad.Your project in one sentence
## Who reads my work
My supervisor, journal reviewers and colleagues outside my field.Your readers
## What I want from Claude
Help me draft emails, minutes and reports. Always tell me when you are not sure of a fact.Your standing request

Ask Claude to write the file with you

Please create a file called About my project.md in my Instructions folder. Ask me four questions first: who I am, what my project is about, who reads my work and what I want from you. Keep the file under 200 words.

Claude asks the four questions, writes the file and saves the file in your Instructions folder. Open the file and correct any errors.

Key tipKeep the file to one page. Correct the file whenever your work changes.

Anthropic. (2026a). How do usage and length limits work? Claude Help Center. https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11647753-how-do-usage-and-length-limits-work

Instruction file two

How I write.md tells Claude which words you avoid and how you sign off

The same request, sent twice: Write to Joseph to confirm the fieldwork dates, 3 to 17 March, and ask Joseph to reply by 25 February on whether the community hall is free on 5 March.

Before: no instruction file

Subject: Exciting fieldwork update!

Hi Joseph,

I hope this email finds you well! I wanted to delve into the next steps of our project, a real game changer in the landscape of island research. We will arrive on 3 March and leave on 17 March. Would the community hall be free on 5 March? Let me know your thoughts by 25 February!

Best wishes

How I write.md

# How I write

## Words I never use
- delve
- landscape
- game changer

## How I sign my emails
Kind regards, Maria

## My style
Plain words. Short paragraphs. British spelling.

After: with the file

Subject: Fieldwork dates for March

Dear Joseph,

I am writing to confirm the fieldwork dates. We arrive on 3 March and leave on 17 March. Could you let me know by 25 February whether the community hall is free on 5 March?

Kind regards,
Maria

Activity

When Claude gets something wrong, write the correction into How I write.md

How I write.md
# How I write ## Words I never use - delve - landscape - game changer ## How I sign my emails Kind regards, Maria ## My style Plain words. Short paragraphs. British spelling.

An example file. The new rule appears at the end of the list.

Try this now

  1. Ask Claude to redraft a short email.
  2. Read the draft and find one word or habit that does not sound like you.
  3. Ask Claude: Please add a rule about this to How I write.md.
  4. Open How I write.md and check the new line.
  5. Send the same request again and compare the two drafts.
Key tipWhen you correct Claude twice for the same habit, write the correction into a file as a rule.

Clear prompt

Write an email to the Finance Office asking when my travel claim will be paid. I submitted the claim on 3 October. The reader handles many claims. Subject line and two short paragraphs, under 120 words.

A free prompt library

The Nextera AI Hub builds a prompt for you in five clicks

Follow along

  2. On your first visit, click Got it, let’s go.
  3. Click I use AI / have access.

Practice

A library prompt asks who you are each time. About my project.md already tells Claude

The Nextera prompt

You are helping a professional working on a team write a post-meeting follow-up email. Fill in: Who I met with: [name / role] What we discussed: [brief summary] What was agreed or decided: [action items, if any] What I want to happen next: [another call / send proposal / their decision / etc.] Under 150 words. Professional but warm.

Excerpt from the Nextera AI Hub prompt “Post-Meeting Follow-Up Email”.

Your turn

  1. Find the Nextera prompt closest to the task you wrote down.
  2. Click Copy Prompt.
  3. Paste the prompt into a new chat inside your project.
  4. Delete what About my project.md already covers.
  5. Fill in the square brackets and send.
  6. Compare the draft with what you would have written yourself.

Nextera is run by a consulting firm in Chicago that sells AI services, so the site links to its own consulting. Many prompts are written for American businesses. Adapt the wording to your work.

RTN purchase and reimbursement process.md
# RTN purchases, the full process ## Standing values, needed on every requisition - Order type: O, Online Payment - Product code, for courses: REGISTRATIONFEE - Tax code: OS ## Before you buy - Start at least four weeks before you need it. - Under EUR 235 excluding VAT, one quotation is enough. Over EUR 235, three quotations are required. ## Things that catch you out - The requisition opens as Parked. Change the status to Active before you save. - Put the website link in the memo.

Set up your own admin folder

  1. Inside your project folder, make a folder called Budget planning, with Procurement and Travel forms inside.
  2. Save every template and every instruction email from Finance or the Travel Office there, as PDF or Word files.
  3. Ask Claude to read the documents and write the procedure as one .md file.
  4. Read the file and correct any step that is wrong.
  5. When a rule changes, ask Claude to update the file the same day.

The recording recreates the steps on screen, using the real files in my folder.

Key tipThe first time you go through a procedure, ask Claude to write each step into a file. The second time, Claude follows the file.

A request that works

I need to pay [what] for [which event or course], [amount]. Please prepare the procurement memo, following RTN purchase and reimbursement process.md. Tell me what to attach.

Claude reads the procedure and the template from the folder, so the request can stay this short. You still read the memo, check every amount and date and attach the files yourself.

Project management

When you forget a step, Claude finds the step in the procedure file you saved

Claude
I saved the requisition. What happens next, and who do I contact?
✳
Following RTN purchase and reimbursement process.md, the requisition now passes through these approvals:
  1. Professor Moncada approves the requisition.
  2. Grants Finance approves the requisition, followed by their manager.
  3. The procurement office issues the purchase order.
  4. Only then, email the online payments officer in Finance with the purchase order number, the amount and the payment link. Copy Grants Finance.
Payments run once a week, so allow two to three weeks. If the requisition seems stuck, check first whether the requisition is waiting for your supervisor’s approval.
Reply to Claude...

Small steps that are easy to forget, all written in the procedure file

  • StatusA requisition opens as Parked. Change the status to Active before saving.
  • Order typeOnline purchases take order type O, Online Payment.
  • TimingStart at least four weeks before a course or conference deadline.
  • The linkPut the website link in the memo, so Finance can pay directly.
  • ContactEmail the online payments officer only after the purchase order exists.
Key tipAsk Claude what comes next at each stage. Claude answers from your procedure file, so the answer matches your University’s rules.

A real example

Each room has an instruction file, written from the corrections I made

Visualising stories, instructions for a new conversation.md
# Visualising stories, instructions for a new conversation ## What the job is Each story takes one recent peer-reviewed article on aid, remittances and wellbeing in small island developing states, explains its main finding in plain academic prose for everyday readers, and shows the idea in one figure. ## Rules Roxane set for visualising stories - Roxane sees the candidates before any is chosen. - Read the whole paper, word for word, before drafting. - 250 words at most. - Every statement is checked against the paper before the story is shown. Nothing is overstated. ## The figure - It must match the other figures on the site in colour and format. Roxane rejected figures in a new style each time.

Excerpts from the instruction file in Work Package 7, shown as written.

roxydewaegh.github.io/FAR-SIDS/#outreach/stories

What went wrong

34 of 37 story cards once needed correcting, mostly because a country-level result had been written up as though it described households.

What changed

The check became a written rule. Each new story is checked against the paper before I see the draft.

If time allows

Five steps take a page from Claude to the internet

  1. In your project, ask Claude: Build a one-page website for my project as a single file called index.html. Use About my project.md for the content.
  2. Go to github.com/new. Type a repository name, keep Public and click Create repository.
  3. Click Add file, then Upload files. Drag in index.html and click Commit changes.
  4. Click Settings, then Pages. Under Source choose Deploy from a branch, choose main and click Save.
  5. Wait up to 10 minutes. Your site appears at yourname.github.io/repository-name.
Key tipPublish only what you would be happy to put on a poster in the corridor.

Working better over time

You might finish fewer tasks while you teach Claude how you work, but once your instructions are written down, you can become more productive

The early weeks

Writing down how you work

We rarely write down how we build an argument, which words we avoid or what evidence we expect. Claude follows only the instructions you write, so in the early weeks you write those files and correct many drafts.

The weeks after

Fewer corrections in every task

Claude applies each rule you write to every later task. Drafts need fewer corrections. You no longer have to remember the steps of a procedure.

Working better over time

Claude’s first two charts looked finished but did not make sense

Version 1

Claude’s first draft

What Claude drew
A curve of the time each task takes, falling as more tasks are done.
Why it did not make sense
The bottom axis mixed tasks with weeks and months. The pink band for teaching Claude sat apart from the line, so the chart never showed what the files cost.
What I asked
I said the graphs were confusing and asked for clearer versions.

Version 2

Claude’s second draft

What Claude drew
Two running totals: hours spent teaching Claude and hours saved, with a yellow area called time gained.
Why it did not make sense
The chart looked precise, but nobody could say what time gained meant. Running totals also read as hours in a single week.
What I asked
I asked what time gained meant. I also asked whether the chart should count tasks completed.

Version 3

The version in this presentation

What Claude drew
Tasks finished each week, with Claude and without Claude.
Why it works
Each line reads one week at a time. The chart shows the slower first weeks as well as the faster weeks after.
Who decided
The idea for this chart came from my question, not from Claude.
Key tipDo not be fooled by a first draft. Read every label and ask what each line means before you use a chart.

Working better over time

Working with Claude builds up like a literature review: each new file connects to the files already there

Key tipClaude can link one file to another. Deciding what each link means remains your work.

Working better over time

A correction I made many times became one rule that Claude reads before every task

CLAUDE.md
# FAR-SIDS. Read this before you touch anything. ## The first rule. **Never add a new point to a sentence with ", and".** "And" is used only to list items ("weddings, funerals and chiefly titles") or to join a second part that is essential to the point and follows logically from the first. Anything else is a new sentence. - Wrong: "This is the largest fall on record, and the OECD expects aid to fall again in 2026." - Right: "This is the largest fall on record. The OECD expects aid to fall again in 2026."

The opening lines of the instruction file in my FAR-SIDS folder, shown as written.

The same sentence, before and after the rule

BeforeThis is the largest fall on record, and the OECD expects aid to fall again in 2026.
AfterThis is the largest fall on record. The OECD expects aid to fall again in 2026.

Without the rule

The same correction, made by hand in every new task.

With the rule

Written once, read by Claude before every task.

Key tipRules reduce mistakes but do not remove them. Claude still breaks rules Claude has been given many times, so read every sentence before you send anything.

Key tipClean the folder every month or two. When a folder contains two drafts of one document, Claude cannot tell which draft is current and may repeat errors you already fixed. Keep only the latest version, with its date in the file name.

Other AI tools

Five tools for finding, reading and organising research

Free

Research Rabbit

You add one paper you trust. Research Rabbit draws a map of the earlier papers that paper cites, the later papers that cite it and the authors who work on the topic.

StudyMeasuredFound

Free basic plan

Elicit

You type a research question. Elicit searches more than 125 million papers and fills a table with what each study measured and found.

Do remittances reduce poverty?
YesPossiblyNo

Free plan

Consensus

You ask a yes or no question. Consensus searches more than 200 million peer reviewed papers and counts how many studies point each way.

→
Answer from your sources [1]

Free with a Google account

NotebookLM

You upload up to 50 of your own sources. NotebookLM answers only from those sources, with a number that opens the passage it used. NotebookLM can also turn the sources into a short audio discussion.

Free

Obsidian

Obsidian keeps your notes as .md files on your own computer. Each note can link to other notes. These are the same kind of .md files that Claude reads in your project folder.

Key tipElicit and Consensus count studies. A count does not tell you whether a study is any good, so open the papers yourself before you cite them.

Consensus. (2026). Consensus: AI search engine for research. https://consensus.app

Elicit. (2026). Pricing. https://elicit.com/pricing

Obsidian. (2026). Obsidian. https://obsidian.md

ResearchRabbit. (2026). Pricing. https://www.researchrabbit.ai/pricing

Other AI tools

Four tools for presenting your research and building online courses

Aid and remittances in Tonga

Free plan, up to 10 slides at a time

Gamma

You type a topic or paste a document. Gamma builds slides, a document or a simple web page that you can export to PowerPoint or PDF.

→

AI podcasts with Academia Premium

Academia.edu

Academia.edu turns a paper you upload into a five minute AI podcast. The site also makes comics and recorded “fireside chats” from papers. Read the terms of use before you upload unpublished work.

Text
Video
Quiz
Flip cards

Paid, with a discount for universities

Articulate 360 (Rise)

Rise builds an online course page by page from ready blocks: text, video, quizzes and flip cards. The finished course loads into a learning platform such as Moodle.

▶?
Drag the word into the gap

Free and open source

H5P

H5P adds interactive videos, quizzes and drag and drop exercises inside Moodle. The UM VLE runs on Moodle, so ask IT Services whether H5P is switched on for your study area.

Key tipFor a short course, start with H5P inside the VLE, because the students already log in there. Consider Articulate only if ISSI wants a polished course open to the public.

One more thing

Claude built this presentation from my instructions. It took 12 versions and my corrections.

0slides
0versions over two days, each one corrected by me
0screenshots, taken by Claude on my laptop, in my browser and from my website’s history
0words of script, drafted for me to speak

What I did

  • 01Decided the audience, the content and the order of the slides
  • 02Pointed Claude to the email, the files and the website for each slide
  • 03Approved the outline before anything was built
  • 04Corrected the content, the visuals and the writing in every version

What Claude did

  • 01Built the slides, animations and walkthroughs I asked for
  • 02Took the screenshots and rebuilt my website’s history
  • 03Drafted the script from my instructions and writing rules
  • 04Applied my corrections, sometimes more than once

Thank you

Which task takes up too much of your time?

Claude can write a draft in seconds from the instructions and files you give Claude. Deciding what the draft should say and checking that the draft is accurate remain our work.
